problem: WayPtNav (CNN predicts waypoints, model-based planner tracks them) uses distance-based heuristic expert supervision that is greedy and not robust to CNN prediction errors, so the robot collides in narrow openings and cluttered spaces. Obstacle padding used to compensate makes narrow doorways impossible to enter.
motivation: CNN waypoint errors are inevitable at test time, and small error margins in narrow passages turn them into collisions. The authors observe that the training supervision itself can be made robust by treating prediction errors as worst-case disturbances in the dynamics, rather than wrapping safety controllers around the learned policy.
key_idea: Generate waypoint supervision with an MPC expert whose cost combines HJ-reachability time-to-reach and time-to-collision value functions computed under worst-case disturbances that model CNN prediction error.
insight: Adding disturbances to the expert dynamics is what buys robustness: without them the expert is 'too optimal', hugging obstacles, and success drops from 63.82% to 49.24% (though it is fastest at 16.19 s). Globally optimal HJ values make the expert less greedy than the heuristic, with the largest gains on Hard tasks (minimum obstacle distance below 0.2 m). The E2E variant trained on this expert performs poorly (8.04%), showing that the nuanced expert behavior is easier to learn as waypoints than as control commands.
method: Robot model: 4D dynamics (x, y, v, phi) with acceleration and turn-rate control; the expert adds disturbances d_x, d_y (bounded circle, 0.05 m/s) and d_phi (0.15 rad/s) to represent CNN error.
HJ value functions: solve static HJ PDEs for time-to-reach (TTR) to the goal set and time-to-collision (TTC) with the obstacle set under worst-case disturbance, using a known training map.
Reachability cost: J(z) = TTR(z) + alpha*(Tmax - TTC(z)), alpha=30, to prioritize collision avoidance.

MPC expert: at each replan (1.5 s horizon), sample a local waypoint grid in the heading direction, build differentially-flat spline trajectories, filter those that violate control constraints, and pick the minimum-cost one.
Data generation: roll out the expert in SD3-like simulation (Stanford S3DIS scans), render the image and record (image, v, omega) with the chosen waypoint as label; 150k samples.

Perception CNN: WayPtNav CNN takes a 224x224 RGB image, goal position and current speeds and regresses a waypoint (x, y, theta) with MSE loss and Adam (lr 1e-4, weight decay 1e-6). Planning and control use a spline plus LQR tracker.

setting.backbone: CNN waypoint predictor (WayPtNav) trained from scratch by supervised learning, plus spline planner and LQR tracker
setting.training_data: 150k image-waypoint pairs from the reachability MPC expert on two S3DIS buildings in simulation
setting.observation: monocular RGB (224x224) plus goal position in the robot frame and current linear/angular speed
setting.action_space: predicted waypoints (x, y, theta) tracked by spline and LQR; underlying controls are acceleration and turn rate
setting.simulator: Stanford S3DIS (Stanford 2D-3D-Semantics) scans rendered in simulation; Turtlebot 2 for hardware
setting.privileged: none at test time (known obstacle map used only for expert supervision during training)

numbers.eval_set_note: 200 navigation tasks in a held-out third S3DIS building, replan 4 Hz
numbers.backbone: CNN trained on reachability expert data
numbers.extra: trained on 150k samples from 2 buildings; disturbances in expert dynamics

numbers.backbone: CNN trained on reachability expert data without disturbances

numbers_note: Custom benchmark, not a standard one; the baselines are WayPtNav-heuristic 52.26% and E2E-heuristic 31.66%. Hardware and difficulty/replan-frequency results are qualitative or in figures only.
results: WayPtNav with the reachability expert reaches 63.82% success on 200 held-out-building tasks versus 52.26% for the heuristic-cost WayPtNav and 49.24% without disturbances, with the lowest jerk (0.94). On a Turtlebot 2 in three unseen narrow-doorway scenarios, the heuristic CNN collided with walls while the reachability CNN reached the goal, without fine-tuning.
limitations: No memory or map, so the robot fails when it must backtrack; success also drops when the room layout differs strongly from training.
Disturbance bounds are set empirically rather than derived, and the expert needs a known map and HJ computation during training; success rates remain modest (~64%).
Evaluation is limited to one held-out simulated building and three hardware scenarios, with no standard benchmark.
